name: Jalapeños
tile_uses: The hot flavor, the jar, the drink
why_now: Jalapeños are peak summer, and in August the heat and color variation is at its widest. Green jalapeños are grassier; red jalapeños (fully ripened) are fruitier and a little hotter. The house flavor this month uses them alongside peppers — but they earn their place in almost every savory dish on the table.
how_to_choose: Firm and glossy, no soft spots
Green is grassy and mild-to-medium; red is fruity and a bit hotter
Streaks of tan or brown on the skin (corking) indicate more heat — a sign of stress on the plant, which concentrates the capsaicin
Smaller jalapeños tend to be hotter than larger ones
buy_this_much: 3–4 jalapeños. Two go into the house flavor; the rest carry the week.
price_note: Jalapeños are inexpensive year-round but at their best now. Look for them at Mexican grocery stores or the farmers market for the freshest selection.

flavor_paths.name: Charred into the sauce
flavor_paths.description: The jar: charred alongside red peppers, blended smooth.

flavor_paths.name: Raw, shaved thin
flavor_paths.description: With lime and flaky salt. The hot flavor.

flavor_paths.name: In the drink
flavor_paths.description: A few rounds in the cooler.

weekday_uses: Shaved thin over halibut or drumsticks
A few rings in the drink
Over fig toast, if you're curious
weekend_use: Charred alongside the peppers for the sauce.
storage: Refrigerator crisper, up to two weeks. They dry out on the counter.
one_thing_to_learn: Heat level in jalapeños varies seed to seed and plant to plant — you can't know from appearance alone. Taste a small piece before adding them to a dish. The seeds and membranes hold most of the heat; removing them makes the pepper significantly milder while keeping the flavor.
market_question: Are these mild or hot this week?
